meta.description: Yes — Carl Jung wrote it, in a letter to Fanny Bowditch, 22 October 1916, first published in R. F. C. Hull's English translation in 1973. The printed text carries no commas.

answer.sourceLine: Confirmed in the primary published source. The sentence closes Jung’s letter to Fanny Bowditch of 22 October 1916, printed in C. G. Jung: Letters, Vol. 1: 1906–1950. Jung wrote to her in German; the familiar English is R. F. C. Hull’s translation, printed in 1973 — and the printed text carries no commas: “Who looks outside dreams; who looks inside awakes.”

source.heading: The letter

docMeta.dd: From the German by R. F. C. Hull. The volume marks its English-original letters “[Original in English]”; this one carries no such marker — unlike the next Bowditch letter, of 30 July 1918 on page 34 — so the English wording is Hull’s.
1973 · Princeton University Press, Bollingen Series XCV:1, ed. Gerhard Adler & Aniela Jaffé

source.excerpt: But your vision will become clear only when you can look into your own heart. … Who looks outside dreams; who looks inside awakes.
trail: Wikiquote’s sourced section ↗ places the line in a letter to Fanny Bowditch dated 22 October 1916, citing C. G. Jung, Letters, Vol. 1: 1906–1950, Bollingen Series XCV:1, edited by Gerhard Adler and Aniela Jaffé, translated by R. F. C. Hull, at page 33.

We then went to the book itself. Full-text search inside the Internet Archive scan of the 1973 Routledge printing ↗, which shares the Bollingen pagination, returns the sentence verbatim — “Who looks outside dreams; who looks inside awakes” — on the page headed “To Fanny Bowditch” with the salutation “Dear Miss Bowditch, 22 October 1916,” immediately before the sign-off.

That page carries no “[Original in English]” marker, though the volume uses one 143 times — including on the next letter to her, “To Fanny Bowditch Katz,” 30 July 1918, on the following page. The title page reads “translations from the German by R. F. C. Hull,” so the English sentence printed here is Hull’s rendering of Jung’s German, not Jung’s own English. See the scan ↗

The earliest edition Open Library ↗ lists for Volume I of the Adler and Jaffé Letters of C. G. Jung is 1973, and the scanned volume’s own front matter says the same — “Volume 1, first published in 1973” — the date that governs the copyright status below. Quote Investigator has no article on this line, so nothing here departs from a specialist finding.
source.excerptNote: The closing lines of Jung’s letter to Fanny Bowditch, 22 October 1916. One intervening sentence is elided here. Note the punctuation as printed — no comma after “outside” or after “inside” — and note that the passage runs directly into Jung’s sign-off, “With best regards.”

source.rightsNote: The letter was written in 1916, but under US law what matters is first publication — and this text first reached print in the 1973 Letters of C. G. Jung, Volume I ↗, long after the cutoff for US public domain by publication date (as of 2026, works published in 1930 or earlier). The wording as printed is therefore in copyright, held by Jung’s estate together with the publisher — and because the English is R. F. C. Hull’s translation of Jung’s German, the translation carries its own copyright layer on top of the underlying letter. Quoted here in brief for attribution and comment.

author.name: Carl Jung
author.heading: Who was Carl Jung?
author.metaLine: 1875–1961 · Swiss psychiatrist · founder of analytical psychology
author.bio: Carl Gustav Jung was born on 26 July 1875 in Kesswil, Switzerland, and died at Küsnacht on 6 June 1961. A psychiatrist and psychotherapist, he founded the school of analytical psychology as a system distinct from Freudian psychoanalysis, built around individuation — the lifelong differentiation of the self out of conscious and unconscious material — along with the collective unconscious, archetypes and synchronicity. He was also a prodigious correspondent, and a great deal of the most quotable Jung comes not from his books but from private letters, collected and published only after his death.

misattribution.heading: The name is right. The punctuation and the sourcing usually aren’t.
misattribution.intro: This is one of the rare celebrity-magnet quotes that survives scrutiny — Jung really did write it. What travels badly is everything around the words: the commas, the source, and the half of the passage that gets cut off.

items.why: The form that circulates — “Who looks outside, dreams; who looks inside, awakes” — adds two commas the book does not have. The 1973 Routledge printing ↗, which shares the pagination of Bollingen XCV:1, prints it as “Who looks outside dreams; who looks inside awakes.”

The line is usually posted with no source at all, or credited flatly to “Carl Jung” as though it were a passage from his work. It is not. Wikiquote’s sourced entry ↗ traces it to a private letter of 22 October 1916; the volume’s own editorial footnote records that James Jackson Putnam had referred the recipient to Jung for treatment in 1912, and the book itself did not appear until 1973, more than a decade after Jung’s death.

Quote cards give the epigram alone. In the letter it is the conclusion of a thought that begins “your vision will become clear only when you can look into your own heart” — counsel to one distressed correspondent, not a general law of the psyche. The scanned volume ↗ shows it running straight into his sign-off.

misattribution.truthLine: Carl Jung really wrote it — to Fanny Bowditch, on 22 October 1916, published in English translation in Letters of C. G. Jung ↗ in 1973. Only the commas belong to the internet.

context.heading: Advice to one woman, not a maxim for everyone
lead: The letter was not written for publication, and it was not written to the world. Its recipient was Fanny Bowditch (1874–1967), daughter of the Harvard physiologist Henry Pickering Bowditch, whom the American neurologist James Jackson Putnam had referred to Jung for treatment in 1912. The volume’s editorial footnote records that she married Dr. Rudolf Katz of Amsterdam in 1916 — and this October 1916 letter still opens “Dear Miss Bowditch,” while the next letter to her in the volume, of 30 July 1918, is headed to “Fanny Bowditch Katz.”

Read in place, the famous line is not a standalone epigram but the last beat of a piece of counsel to a specific person who had told Jung she needed to see her situation clearly. He answers that clarity is not available from the outside. Stripped of that setting and set in a serif font over a mountain, it becomes something more sweeping than what he actually wrote.
detailsBody: The volume’s editors note that in the letters Jung wrote in English their intervention was “limited mainly to punctuation” — but this is not one of those letters. Here the English is R. F. C. Hull’s translation from Jung’s German, so the semicolon a reader meets is a translator’s choice made for the 1973 edition rather than a mark Jung set down in 1916.

Either way the printed punctuation is an artifact of publication, not of the writing desk — which makes the extra commas in the internet version doubly worth flagging. They are not a variant reading from some other edition; they are a later tidying of a text that had already passed through a translator.
